facts.statement: The genus Dianopachysaurus was first named by a team of researchers including Jun Liu and Olivier Rieppel in 2011.
facts.quote: It was first named by Jun Liu, Olivier Rieppel, Da-Yong Jiang, Jonathan C. Aitchison, Ryosuke Motani, Qi-Yue Zhang, Chang-Yong Zhou and Yuan-Yuan Sun in 2011

facts.statement: Dianopachysaurus lived during the lower Middle Triassic (Anisian age) in Yunnan Province, southwestern China.
facts.quote: Dianopachysaurus is an extinct genus of pachypleurosaur known from the lower Middle Triassic (Anisian age) of Yunnan Province, southwestern China.

facts.statement: The fossils of Dianopachysaurus were found in the Middle Triassic Guanling Formation Lagerstätte.
facts.quote: It was found in the Middle Triassic Lagerstätte of the Guanling Formation.

facts.statement: Dianopachysaurus belongs to the family Keichousauridae.
facts.quote: Both belong to the family Keichousauridae.

facts.statement: The known fossil skeleton of Dianopachysaurus measured 14.3 cm from the nose to the 17th caudal vertebra.
facts.quote: It measured 14.3 cm long from nose tip to the last caudal vertebra known, although the end of the tail is missing after the 17th caudal vertebra.

facts.statement: The total body length of Dianopachysaurus is estimated to have been about 20 cm.
facts.quote: It is estimated to have measured about to 20 cm in total body length.

facts.statement: Dianopachysaurus had a broad, flat skull with eyes positioned far forward and a snout shorter than the postorbital region.
facts.quote: The skull is broad and flat, with the eyes quite far forward and the snout shorter than the postorbital region.

facts.statement: The nostrils of Dianopachysaurus were small, measuring only 1.5 mm in length and having an almost square or trapezoid shape.
facts.quote: The nares are small, only 1.5 mm long, and almost square or trapezoid.

facts.statement: The eye socket of Dianopachysaurus was large, with a diameter of 6 mm, but lacked scleral ossicles.
facts.quote: The orbit is large, at 6 mm in diameter, but has no scleral ossicles present.

facts.statement: The upper temporal openings of Dianopachysaurus were only 4.5 mm long and relatively small.
facts.quote: The upper temporal fenestrae are only 4.5 mm long, and much thinner, making them relatively small.

facts.statement: The skeleton of Dianopachysaurus includes 20 cervical, 19 dorsal, 3 sacral, and at least 17 caudal vertebrae.
facts.quote: 20 cervical vertebrae, 19 dorsal vertebrae, 3 sacral vertebrae and at least 17 caudal vertebrae are present.

facts.statement: The dorsal vertebrae of Dianopachysaurus lacked elongated transverse processes but had very pachyostotic zygapophyses.
facts.quote: The dorsal vertebrae have no elongated transverse processes, but the zygapophyses are very pachyostotic.

facts.statement: The dorsal ribs of Dianopachysaurus were single-headed, significantly elongate, and highly pachyostotic.
facts.quote: The dorsal ribs are single-headed, significantly more elongate, and highly pachyostotic.

facts.statement: The humerus of Dianopachysaurus was 10 mm long and had unequal attachments for the ulna and radius.
facts.quote: The humeri are 10 mm long, and have unequal attachments for the ulnae and radii.

facts.statement: The ulna and radius of Dianopachysaurus were both 5 mm long and the ulna was no wider than the radius.
facts.quote: The ulnae is no wider than the radii are, and they are both 5 mm long.

facts.statement: The femur of Dianopachysaurus was 14 mm long, slender, slightly S-shaped, and had distinct striations on both ends.
facts.quote: The femurs are slender and slightly sigmoid, with distinct striations on both ends. They are 14 mm long.

facts.statement: The fibula of Dianopachysaurus was slightly longer than the tibia, measuring 6.5 mm compared to 6 mm.
facts.quote: The fibulae are slightly longer than the tibiae, at 6.5 rather than 6 mm long.

facts.statement: Preserved foot phalanges in Dianopachysaurus show pointed tips that may have been claws, with a probable formula of 2,3,4,5,4.
facts.quote: Enough phalanges are preserved in their original positions, however, to let us see that all the most distal phalanges have pointed tips, which may originally have been claws, and to give a probable phalangeal formula for the foot of 2,3,4,5,4.

facts.statement: Dianopachysaurus is classified within the superorder Sauropterygia, order Nothosauroidea, suborder Pachypleurosauria, and family Keichousauridae.
facts.quote: superordo: Sauropterygia ordo: Nothosauroidea subordo: Pachypleurosauria familia: Keichousauridae

facts.statement: The type species of Dianopachysaurus is Dianopachysaurus dingi, described by Liu et al. in 2011.
facts.quote: subdivision: D. dingi Liu et al., 2011 (especie tipo)

facts.statement: Researchers hypothesize that pachypleurosaurs originated in the eastern Tethys Ocean (South China) before spreading to the western Tethys (Europe).
facts.quote: Pachypleurosaurs are hypothesized to have originated in the eastern Tethys Ocean (South China) before spreading and diversifying in the western Tethys in what is now Europe.

rejected.statement: Dianopachysaurus represents an early stage in the radiation of pachypleurosaurs, filling a significant gap in their evolutionary history.
rejected.quote: Dianopachysaurus represents an early stage in the radiation of pachypleurosaurs and its early age fills in much of the gap.
